article.plain_text:
This week the web changed shape, and almost nobody announced it.
On Thursday, Sierra released Poppy 1.0, a standard that lets a shop tell your personal agent how to work with it. The same day, Meta quietly put Muse into Chrome as a side panel extension, with no announcement at all. And on Monday, Forter updated its checkout data with the receipts: Muse already places more orders than ChatGPT and Google combined.
Three separate events. One story. The agent stopped being a place you visit. It became the way the store talks to you.
A file every store now publishes
Poppy is short for the Personal Agent Protocol. It is a small file a business publishes at a fixed address on its own site, /.well-known/poppy.json. The file says who the business is, how an agent signs a customer in, what the agent may ask for, and where its systems live.
Sierra built it with Meta. Version 1.0 arrived on November 13, five weeks after the first draft. Sixty new companies joined as design partners, bringing the total past 100. The names include Cisco, Delta Air Lines, Intuit, Salesforce, Twilio, and Zoom.
The part that matters most is Shopify. Every Shopify store now publishes a Poppy file automatically, with no work from the merchant. Shopify runs stores in more than 175 countries. An independent check on November 15 found the file live on 104 of 109 Shopify stores sampled, and on none of 20 stores on other platforms.
Muse now looks for Poppy first on every site it visits. Before it reads the page, it reads the file. The store tells the agent the rules before the agent starts shopping.
Poppy also links to the Universal Commerce Protocol, which handles carts and checkout. Poppy opens the door. The protocol carries the basket through it.
The receipts at checkout
A standard means little until orders flow through it. Forter, a fraud prevention company that watches checkout data across a large network of merchants, published the numbers on Monday.
Forter first detected Muse orders on September 21. That week, agentic orders jumped 229 percent month over month, and Muse placed more than half of them. In the week of October 19, Muse placed 49 percent of all agentic orders on the network.
The lead has held. Muse now places 2.9 times as many orders a day as ChatGPT and Google combined. In November, the average agentic order was 204 dollars. These are real purchases, not test carts.
The shape matters as much as the size. Agents that drive a merchant's own checkout pages, the same pages a person sees, went from 1.2 percent of agentic orders in the week of August 17 to 80.5 percent in the week of November 2.
Muse bought at 74 percent of the stores that received any agentic order at all. ChatGPT Agent, the browsing agent Forter tracks separately from OpenAI's protocol checkout, bought at 45 percent.
Read that plainly. In eight weeks, the agent that shops the way a person shops went from undetected to the largest buyer on the network. The stores did not rebuild for it.
The browser opened its own door
The third event this week happened without a press release. Meta published "Muse from Meta" on the Chrome Web Store. It puts Muse in Chrome's side panel, beside the page you are already reading. The listing was updated again on November 16, to version 2.0.77. Meta has still said nothing about it in public.
The difference is the address. Until now, Muse ran in a cloud browser, separate from yours, with your logins held in a vault. The extension runs Muse in your own Chrome, using the sites you are already signed into. No re-signing in. The shortcut Alt+Shift+C calls it up from any page.
The listing promises action approvals, an activity log, and connections you can revoke. It also carries the honest warning: Muse may be inaccurate or take unexpected actions, so check in and keep it on track.
That trade is the real story. The cloud browser kept your computer out of the loop. Your own browser gives the agent reach: it can act as you, on sites where you are already logged in. Reach goes up. So does what is in reach.
The interface test
On Monday, Ethan Mollick, a professor at Wharton who writes about working with agents, posted the comparison that ties the week together. He wrote that OpenAI's Dot is capable but falls further behind Muse and Duet on interface: a single-threaded conversation, no inline flourishes like maps, and no way to see what tasks it has been assigned.
That is the test every agent now faces, and it is not a benchmark score. It is whether you can see what the agent is doing. A map inside the chat. A task list you can watch. A store that answers in the agent's own language.
What to do with this week
If you run a store on Shopify, open your own /.well-known/poppy.json today and read what it lets agents do. You already published it. Know what it says.
If you shop with Muse, try one real errand in the Chrome side panel this week. Start small, watch the activity log, and keep the approval step on.
If you doubted agents would ever do more than chat, look at the Forter numbers again. The checkout changed first. The standards and the browser are catching up.
The web spent thirty years building pages for people. This week it started building a front door for the agent. The stores that open it first will be the ones the agent shops at first.
Follow @Musecases for more

The agent, the single transaction and the fee route nobody can change.
Every day, a handful of posts on X take off faster than anything around them. A joke, a photo, a piece of news. Within minutes someone launches a coin on it, and the person who posted it gets nothing.
AgentPaid is the first AI agent built to do the opposite. It catches a post as it takes off, launches its coin on pump.fun in seconds, and sends every creator fee from that coin to the person who posted it. Automatically, and for good.
Three pieces of technology make that possible, and they rarely meet in one product: an agent that judges a post the way a trader would, a launch that writes the fee route into the coin at the moment it is created, and a payout that needs nothing from the person being paid.
An agent that reads posts the way a trader does
Keyword bots launch on anything that matches a word. AgentPaid reads the post itself: its text, its picture, its likes, reposts, replies and views, and how many minutes ago it went up.
It measures how fast a post is moving. That means likes per minute between two readings, smoothed so one spike does not fool it, alongside the average since the post went live. A post moving faster than everything around it gets the agent’s attention. A post that only looks busy does not.
Before any model sees a post, a hard safety gate runs. Tragedies, anything involving minors, adult content, scams and posts pushing another token’s contract address are rejected outright. Only then does the language model decide.
If the answer is yes, the agent names the coin from the post’s own words and picks a ticker from its most memorable word. If the answer is no, the post gets a short roast instead of a coin. The agent is selective by design, because a launchpad that says yes to everything is just a faucet.
Every coin starts with its route already written
This is the part that makes AgentPaid different from every tool that simply launches coins.
On pump.fun, every X account has its own fee account, derived from that account’s X user ID. It exists whether or not the person has ever touched crypto. AgentPaid creates the coin and points 100% of its creator fee at that account in the same transaction. For most names it all fits in one Solana transaction: the coin, its fee-sharing configuration and the share that sends every fee to the author.
There is no window in which the coin exists but the fees go somewhere else. From its first trade, the coin pays the person who posted.
Set once, for good
pump.fun lets a coin’s fee route be changed a single time. AgentPaid uses that one change at launch to point the fees at the author. After that the route is fixed. Nobody can redirect it later, including us.
You do not have to take our word for it. Every coin’s fee-sharing configuration is an account on Solana. Open it and you will see one shareholder: the author’s X fee account.
Payouts nobody has to ask for
Creator fees collect in the coin’s creator vault as people trade. Moving them to the shareholders is a permissionless instruction on pump.fun, so anyone can trigger it. AgentPaid’s crank does it every few minutes, for every coin, and the fees land in the author’s X account by themselves.
The author does not sign up, connect a wallet or press a button. Their fees simply arrive.
Three ways in, one engine
The agent watches X on its own and launches the posts it catches.
Anyone can also point it at a post. Reply @useAgentPaid under any post on X and the agent reads the post you replied to. Within a minute it answers with a live coin for the author, or with a roast. Each tag gets exactly one answer, and each post can only ever become one coin.
On useagentpaid.fun you can paste any post, watch the agent decide, and launch the coin it named with a single signature. Your wallet only ever signs one plain transfer. A one-time launch key creates the coin, locks the route, makes your first buy if you want one, and returns every unused lamport and every token to you. If you close the page halfway, the launch picks up where it stopped.
Why it matters
For the people who post, AgentPaid turns the moment they create into income they never had to ask for.
For traders, it is the earliest possible coin on a post that is taking off. It is also the one the author has every reason to share, because it pays them.
Every launch is on chain, and every route can be checked. That is the whole idea: an agent that catches the moment, and a coin that pays the person who made it.

Everyone is talking about AI agents. Very few people explain what an agent actually is, or what you have to do to make one work well.
So let's start there, and then go level by level. Every level has one running example, the exact files and commands, and the mistake that keeps people stuck. Everything here is real Claude Code syntax you can copy today.
First: what an agent actually is
An agent is a loop. That is it.
Gather context. Read files, search the code, look at the error.
Act. Edit a file, run a command, call a tool.
Verify. Run the tests, check the output, compare against the goal.
Repeat until the goal is met.
 
A chatbot does step 2 once and hands the result to you. An agent runs the whole loop by itself.
Claude Fable 5.2 is the strongest model you can put in that loop in Claude Code. Anthropic's docs describe Fable models as built for tasks larger than a single sitting: they sustain long autonomous sessions, investigate before acting, and verify their work more often than smaller models.
But the model is only one part. The loop is only as good as three things you control:
The context it starts with
The tools it can reach
The checks that tell it whether it is done
Every level below upgrades one of those three. That is the whole framework.
Never used Claude Code? Your first 10 minutes
You do not need to be a developer to follow along.
Install it. Use the one-line installer from the official Claude Code page, or open the Claude desktop app and switch to the Code tab.
Open a folder. Make a folder for your project, open a terminal in it and type claude. Say yes when it asks whether to trust the folder.
Pick the model. Type /model fable.
Give yourself an undo button. Send this as your first message: "Set this folder up as a Git project and save a checkpoint with a short note after every change." Now you can always say "go back to the last checkpoint." Claude Code also has its own rewind: press Esc twice on an empty prompt.
The running example for this article: your app has an Orders page, and users want to export their orders as a CSV file. We will build that feature at every level and watch what changes.
 
Level 1: The Chatbot
You open Claude in the browser and type: "Write a function that converts a list of orders to CSV."
You get a decent function. You paste it into your project. It uses a field name your code does not have. You paste the error back. It fixes that. Now the dates come out in the wrong format. Ten rounds later, it works. Mostly.
Why it is slow: the model never sees your code and never runs anything. Steps 1 and 3 of the loop, context and verification, are done by you, by hand, through copy-paste. You are the agent. The model is an autocomplete.
Move up: install Claude Code, open it in your project folder, and run /model fable.
Level 2: The Prompter
Now Fable is in your project. It can read files, edit them and run commands. The loop exists.
But Level 2 users still talk to it like a chatbot:
"write a function that converts orders to csv"
"now add a button"
"now make the button call the function"
"the test is failing, fix it"
Four prompts, four waits, and you are still the one deciding every step. You are using an agent as a typing assistant.
The fix is the single most important skill in this article: describe the outcome, not the steps. Anthropic's own guidance for Fable says exactly this.
 
A good agent prompt has three parts:
1. The goal, in user terms.
"Users need to export their orders as CSV from the Orders page."
2. What "done" means. This is the part almost everyone skips, and it is what makes the agent's verification step work.
"Done means: a button on the Orders page downloads a CSV with date, order ID, items and total. It respects the current filters. Tests cover an empty order list and item names that contain commas. All existing tests still pass."
3. Where to look first.
"Look at how the existing PDF export works and follow the same pattern."
Send that once. Fable reads the PDF export, finds the data layer, builds the endpoint and the button, writes the tests, runs them, fixes what fails, and reports back.
The mistake that keeps people here: interrupting. When the agent is investigating for a minute before editing anything, that is not wasted time. That is step 1 of the loop. Let it run.
Level 3: The Context Builder
At Level 2, every new session starts from zero. Fable has to rediscover that you use pnpm, that tests live in a certain folder, that the PDF export is the pattern to follow. Sometimes it guesses wrong.
Level 3 users write it down once. In Claude Code, run /init. It creates CLAUDE.md in your project. Claude Code loads this file at the start of every session. It is the agent's standing context.
 
What belongs in CLAUDE.md:
Commands. How to install, test, lint and run the app. The agent uses these to verify its own work.
A map. Where the main things live, in a few lines.
Rules that differ from the defaults. "Never edit /generated." "Money is stored in cents." "Exports follow the pattern in src/exports/pdf."
Known traps. The thing that broke last month.
What does not belong:
Anything the agent can learn by reading the code in seconds.
Generic advice like "write clean code." It changes nothing.
Long step-by-step procedures. Those go into skills (Level 5), which load only when needed.
Every line in CLAUDE.md is read in every session, so keep it short and specific.
The habit that makes this work: whenever the agent makes the same mistake twice, add one line to CLAUDE.md. After a few weeks, the file reads like onboarding notes from your best teammate.
Level 4: The Planner
The most expensive agent mistake is not a bad line of code. It is twenty minutes of good code in the wrong direction.
Level 4 users press Shift+Tab in Claude Code to cycle into plan mode. Fable investigates, writes a plan, and waits for your approval before it edits anything.
Reading a plan well takes about two minutes. Check three things:
Which files will it touch? A file you did not expect is a red flag. Ask why.
How will it verify? If the plan does not say which tests or commands it will run, tell it.
What is it assuming? "I'll add a CSV library." Do you want a new dependency? If you already have one, say so.
For the CSV export, a typical correction looks like: "Don't add a new library, we already use papaparse. And the export must respect the date filter, not just the status filter." Two sentences that save a rewrite.
For genuinely hard tasks, raise the effort. Fable 5.2 runs at medium effort by default: /effort high.
The mistake that keeps people here: approving plans without reading them. Plan mode only helps if you actually push back.
Level 5: The Toolsmith
Levels 3 and 4 upgrade the agent's context and direction. Level 5 upgrades what it can reach and what it knows how to do.
Skills: procedures the agent loads when needed
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file inside .claude/skills/. It holds a procedure: how you write release notes, how you deploy, how you review a migration. Its description is always visible to the agent, but the full body loads only when the skill is used, so it costs almost nothing until needed.
Here is a real one. Save it as .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md:
---
description: Writes release notes from changes since the last tag. Use when asked for release notes or a changelog entry.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

## Changes since last release
!`git log $(git describe --tags --abbrev=0)..HEAD --oneline`

## Instructions
Group the changes into Features, Fixes and Internal.
One line each, written for users, not developers.
Leave out Internal unless asked.
The line starting with ! runs the command and inlines its output before the agent sees the skill. Type /release-notes and the agent starts with the real list of changes already in front of it.
The rule of thumb: CLAUDE.md holds facts that are always true. Skills hold procedures you run sometimes.
MCP: connect the agent to your real tools
MCP servers give the agent tools beyond your files: your error tracker, your database, a browser. Adding one is a single command, run in your terminal:
claude mcp add --transport http sentry https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp
Then run /mcp inside Claude Code, select the server and authenticate.
Now when a user reports "the CSV export crashes," you do not paste a stack trace. You say "fix the CSV export crash from Sentry," and the agent reads the real error, finds the cause and fixes it.
The mistake here: connecting everything. Every connected server loads its tool names into every session and takes context space. Connect what you actually use.
Level 6: The Manager
Up to now, one agent did everything in one conversation. At Level 6 you split the work.
Subagents
A subagent runs in its own context window, with its own instructions and its own allowed tools. It does a focused job and returns only a summary to your main conversation. That is the real reason they matter: the noisy work (search results, test logs, long file reads) stays out of your main context, which keeps the main agent sharp in long sessions.
Here is a reviewer that checks finished work before the main agent calls it done. Save it as .claude/agents/reviewer.md:
 
 
Notice two choices. The reviewer runs on sonnet, a cheaper model, because reviewing a diff does not need Fable. And the description says when to use it, because that is how the main agent decides to delegate. You can also call it directly: "use the reviewer subagent on this change." You do not have to write the file yourself either: describe the helper you want and ask Claude to create it in .claude/agents/.
Good jobs for subagents: investigating a bug across a big codebase, running and reading long test output, reviewing. Bad jobs: quick back-and-forth edits, which are faster in the main conversation.
Hooks
CLAUDE.md asks the agent to follow rules. Hooks enforce them. A hook is a command Claude Code runs automatically at a specific moment, every time, whether the model remembers or not.
This one, in .claude/settings.json, formats every file right after the agent edits it:
 
Other useful hooks: a PreToolUse hook that blocks edits to protected files (a script that exits with code 2 blocks the action and tells the agent why), and a Stop hook that checks the tests pass before the agent is allowed to finish. The Stop version uses an agent-based hook, which the docs mark as experimental.
Fable as the advisor
You do not have to run Fable on every step. Run a faster model as the main worker and attach Fable as its advisor: /advisor fable.
The main model handles routine work and consults Fable at decision points: before committing to an approach, when an error keeps coming back, and before declaring the task done. You get Fable's judgment where it matters without paying Fable rates for every file read.
 
The mistake here: launching many subagents in parallel for everything. Each one returns results into your main context, and that adds up. Delegate the noisy, focused jobs, not every step.
Level 7: The Owner
At Level 7 the agent runs without a chat window.
Run it from scripts and CI
The -p flag runs Claude Code non-interactively: one prompt in, one result out, exit code for success or failure.
Explain a build failure from a log file:
cat build-error.txt | claude -p "concisely explain the root cause of this build error"
Fix failing tests with only the tools you allow:
claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit"
Three flags worth knowing for automation:
--bare skips your local hooks, skills, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md, so the run behaves the same on every machine. Recommended for CI. It needs an API key in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
--output-format json returns structured output, including total_cost_usd, so your scripts can track spend.
--permission-mode auto --permission-prompts none for unattended runs: a classifier reviews actions, and anything that would wait for a human is denied instead of hanging.
Run it on a schedule
Inside a session, /loop repeats a prompt on an interval, for example /loop 5m check whether the deploy finished. For work that should run with your laptop closed, Claude Code has cloud scheduled tasks that run on a schedule, on an API call or on a GitHub event.
Build your own
The Claude Agent SDK gives you the same agent loop, tools and context management that power Claude Code, as Python and TypeScript packages. When your workflow outgrows a script, that is the next step.
The mistake here: automating before Levels 3 to 6 are solid. An unattended agent with no CLAUDE.md, no tests to verify against and no hooks will do the wrong thing confidently, at 3am, with nobody watching.
The hidden limit: context
Every level above depends on one resource most people never look at: the context window. It is the agent's working memory. Everything lives there: your messages, its answers, every file it read, every tool result, CLAUDE.md, the tool lists of your MCP servers.
When it gets crowded, quality drops. The agent loses track of early instructions, repeats work, and gets slower. People say "Claude got dumber in this session." Usually it just got full.
Fable 5.2 runs with a 1M-token context window by default. That is huge, and it is exactly why people stop paying attention to it. A bigger window still rewards a clean one.
Type /context in Claude Code. It shows your current usage as a colored grid and suggests what to cut: heavy tools, an oversized memory file, warnings when you are close to the limit.
 
Four habits keep it clean:
One task, one conversation. Finished the CSV export? /clear before you start the next feature.
Compact long sessions on purpose. /compact summarizes the conversation so far and frees space. You can tell it what to keep: /compact keep the decisions about the export format.
Rewind instead of arguing. If the last few turns went wrong, press Esc twice on an empty prompt (or type /rewind) and go back to before the mistake, instead of piling corrections on top.
Push noisy work into subagents. Their logs and search results stay in their own context. Only the summary comes back.
The cheat sheet
Save this one.
 
Keys
Shift+Tab cycles permission modes: Manual, accept edits, plan.
Esc stops Claude mid-turn. The work done so far is kept.
Esc Esc on an empty prompt opens the rewind menu.
Ctrl+O opens the transcript viewer: every tool call, with the model used.
Ctrl+B sends running commands and agents to the background.
Ctrl+R searches your prompt history.
Commands
/init writes CLAUDE.md for your project.
/model fable switches to Fable 5.2. /effort high for hard tasks.
/context shows what is filling the context window.
/clear starts a fresh conversation. /compact summarizes and frees space.
/rewind goes back to an earlier point in code and conversation.
/mcp manages connected servers. /hooks shows your hooks.
/advisor fable attaches Fable as the advisor to a faster model.
/usage shows cost and plan limits.
How not to burn your limits with Fable
Fable is the most capable Claude model and it is priced like it. Depending on your plan, Fable usage can be billed to separate usage credits instead of your normal limits. The /model picker shows "Requires usage credits" on the Fable row when that applies.
Practical rules:
Put Fable where judgment matters. Ambiguous bugs, architecture, long autonomous tasks.
Use cheaper models for mechanical work, including subagents. Set model: sonnet or model: haiku in their files.
Use /advisor fable when you want Fable's judgment without running it on every step.
Match effort to the task. /effort low for simple jobs, /effort high for hard ones.
Watch automated runs. In -p mode and in Agent SDK apps that do not show the consent prompt, Claude Code bills Fable usage to credits without asking. Set a cap with --max-budget-usd.
Check your spend with /usage.
The checklist
One action per level. Do the next one on your list this week.
Install Claude Code and run /model fable.
Rewrite your next prompt as goal + definition of done + where to look.
Run /init and cut CLAUDE.md down to commands, map, rules and traps.
Use plan mode (Shift+Tab) on your next big change and push back on one assumption.
Turn one procedure you repeat into a skill. Connect one MCP server you actually use.
Add a reviewer subagent and one hook.
Put one claude -p command into a script or CI job.
The difference between people who say "AI agents are overhyped" and people who get real work out of them is not the model. Everyone reading this has access to the same Fable. The difference is the context, tools and checks around it.
Reply with your level, 1 to 7.
 
Save this and come back when you are ready for the next level.
Next, I am publishing the full CLAUDE.md template I would give any team starting with Fable. Follow so you do not miss it.
Commands and file formats follow the Claude Code documentation at the time of writing. Fable access, pricing and plan limits vary by account and can change.

AI-Powered Semiconductor Design Starts with Better Training Data: 652 Verified Analog & RF Device Layouts from Xpert Systems
Introducing SEMI-DEV-001: A High-Fidelity Curated Dataset for Training, Fine-Tuning, and Evaluating AI Models and EDA Agents in Semiconductor Design
The Next Frontier of AI Is Semiconductor Engineering
Artificial intelligence is transforming software development, scientific discovery, mechanical engineering, and industrial automation. Semiconductor design represents another major opportunity.
AI models are increasingly being explored for circuit generation, physical layout, design-rule verification, electronic design automation (EDA), and automated design optimization.
Yet one major challenge remains: Where do we obtain the high-quality, technically correct semiconductor design data needed to train these models?
Unlike natural language or general-purpose programming, semiconductor layouts must satisfy precise manufacturing constraints.
A semiconductor layout cannot simply look correct.
Its geometry must comply with fabrication rules. Its electrical connections must match the intended circuit. Its dimensions must correspond to valid devices. Its layers must be compatible with the target process technology.
A seemingly minor spacing violation, missing via, incorrect enclosure, or disconnected terminal can invalidate an otherwise plausible design.
This creates a fundamental challenge for AI development.
Models must learn not only how semiconductor devices are drawn but also how to generate layouts that satisfy real engineering constraints.
At Xpert Systems Inc., we are addressing this challenge through high-fidelity curated semiconductor datasets designed specifically for AI model training, fine-tuning, benchmarking, evaluation, and agent development.
Our latest dataset, SEMI-DEV-001, provides 652 original analog and RF device layouts across two open semiconductor process design kits.
Every device has passed its applicable documented quality checks.
This is more than a collection of semiconductor images.
It is a structured engineering dataset connecting physical geometry, device parameters, electrical netlists, verification results, and machine-readable metadata.
1. Why Analog and RF Layout Data Is So Difficult to Obtain
Digital semiconductor design has benefited from decades of automation.
Synthesis tools translate hardware descriptions into logic circuits. Placement-and-routing software organizes standard cells and interconnects. Verification tools identify many classes of design errors.
Analog and radio-frequency design remain more challenging.
Analog circuits frequently require carefully controlled device geometry, matching, parasitic behavior, and physical relationships between components.
Consider a simple MOSFET layout.
The design depends on several parameters, including transistor width, channel length, number of fingers, device type, and process-specific layer requirements.
Changing one parameter may require modifications to diffusion regions, contacts, gate structures, metal connections, and surrounding geometry.
Now consider a spiral inductor.
Its physical behavior depends on the number of turns, inner diameter, trace width, and spacing. These features influence inductance and other electrical characteristics.
An AI model trained on visual examples alone may learn to imitate the appearance of these structures without understanding the rules governing their construction.
This is where traditional image datasets become insufficient.
Semiconductor AI requires geometry that can be checked, electrical connections that can be verified, and design parameters that can be traced back to the resulting layout.
Unfortunately, many production semiconductor layouts are proprietary and governed by foundry confidentiality agreements.
Public examples are comparatively limited, and their documentation and verification quality can vary substantially.
SEMI-DEV-001 is designed to address this data bottleneck.
2. Introducing SEMI-DEV-001: 652 Original Analog and RF Device Layouts
SEMI-DEV-001 is a curated collection of analog and RF device layouts developed using two open process design kits:
SkyWater SKY130: A 130-nanometer semiconductor process.
GlobalFoundries GF180MCU: A 180-nanometer semiconductor process.
The collection includes 404 SKY130 devices and 248 GF180MCU devices.
Together, they form a 652-device dataset covering six fundamental device categories.
MOSFET Transistors — 336 Layouts
The dataset contains 240 SKY130 transistor layouts and 96 GF180MCU transistor layouts.
Variations include NMOS and PMOS devices, channel dimensions, and configurations containing one to eight fingers.
The SKY130 examples include standard-, low-, and high-threshold-voltage device variants. The GF180 collection also includes 5 V devices.
These layouts provide training examples for understanding how transistor parameters translate into manufacturable geometry.
Poly Resistors — 144 Layouts
The resistor collection includes 72 layouts for each process.
Variations cover resistor width, length, and serpentine configurations with one to four segments.
The collection includes SKY130 poly and high-resistance poly structures, along with GF180 unsalicided P+ and N+ poly devices.
These examples allow models to learn relationships between physical resistor dimensions and estimated electrical resistance.
MIM Capacitors — 36 Layouts
Metal-insulator-metal capacitors are widely used in analog and mixed-signal applications.
SEMI-DEV-001 includes 24 SKY130 MIM capacitor layouts and 12 GF180MCU layouts.
Examples cover single devices and capacitor arrays, including 1×1, 2×1, and 2×2 configurations.
The SKY130 examples include its two supported MIM layers.
These structures are useful for models learning capacitor geometry, array construction, and device-level connectivity.
MOM Capacitors — 72 Layouts
Metal-oxide-metal capacitors use patterned metal structures to create capacitance.
The dataset includes 36 MOM capacitor layouts for each process.
Variations include metal stacks containing two to four layers, different finger counts, and finger lengths.
These examples support parameter-to-geometry learning and capacitance-estimation research.
Spiral Inductors — 48 Layouts
The collection contains 24 spiral inductor layouts for each process.
Examples vary from 1.5 to 4.5 turns, with inner diameters ranging from 30 to 100 micrometers, along with different trace widths.
Spiral inductors are particularly interesting for AI-assisted RF design because their performance is strongly influenced by physical geometry.
Guard Rings — 16 Layouts
The collection includes eight guard-ring layouts per process.
Both single P-type rings and double P/N ring configurations are represented.
Guard rings are important building blocks in analog physical design, where isolation and substrate-related considerations affect circuit behavior.
Together, these six categories provide diverse, parameterized examples for training AI systems on fundamental analog and RF layout structures.
3. Every Device Includes More Than Physical Geometry
A defining feature of SEMI-DEV-001 is that each device is delivered as a structured engineering package.
The seven accompanying file types allow models and developers to examine different representations of the same design.
GDSII layout files
Each device includes a .gds file containing the physical layout geometry, using a 1 nm database unit.
GDSII is a standard interchange format for semiconductor physical layout data.
OASIS layout files
Each device also includes an .oas representation.
The dataset's quality checks verify that the OASIS representation matches the corresponding GDS layout.
SPICE netlists
A .spice file records the device's intended electrical representation, including relevant process-model names and device dimensions.
This creates a relationship between physical layout and electrical connectivity.
Design-rule verification reports
Each device includes a _drc.txt report documenting checks against the official open design-rule decks, supplemented by an independent Python checker.
Layout-versus-netlist or connectivity reports
Each device includes an _lvs.txt report documenting the applicable layout-versus-netlist or connectivity verification.
Layout preview images
PNG previews provide visual representations suitable for dataset exploration, inspection, and vision-oriented AI experiments.
Machine-readable metadata
JSON files contain device parameters, terminal information, dimensions, physical area, layers used, electrical estimates, and quality-control results.
This combination is especially valuable for multimodal AI.
A model can be trained to connect a numerical design specification to its geometry, associate physical structures with electrical descriptions, or interpret verification outcomes.
Instead of learning from unrelated examples, the model receives multiple synchronized views of the same engineered device.
4. The Most Important Difference: Engineering Verification
Many AI datasets are assessed primarily through completeness, formatting, or annotation quality.
Semiconductor design requires another level of validation.
A visually convincing layout may still violate manufacturing rules.
SEMI-DEV-001 incorporates a multi-stage quality-control process.
Design Rule Checking
All 652 devices were checked using the official open process rule decks through KLayout.
The verification includes SKY130's applicable rule decks and the GF180MCU full design-rule deck.
Reported result: Zero DRC errors across all 652 devices under the documented verification scope.
Independent Python Rule Checker
Xpert Systems also implemented a separate Python checker covering key width, spacing, enclosure, and area constraints.
This creates a second verification layer.
All 652 devices passed these checks without errors.
Layout-versus-Netlist Verification
For transistors, resistors, and MIM capacitors, the generated geometry is extracted and compared with its electrical description.
The dataset reports successful matching across all 516 devices in these categories, using the applicable checking procedures.
The verification also includes foundry-style GF180 checks, with documented device-level treatment for MIM structures.
Connectivity Verification
For MOM capacitors, spiral inductors, and guard rings, the verification process checks connections and identifies shorts or floating metal.
All 136 devices in these categories passed the documented connectivity checks.
Testing the Checkers Themselves
Verification software must also be tested.
The SEMI-DEV-001 development process deliberately introduced invalid designs to confirm that the quality-control system could detect them.
The documentation reports agreement between the independent Python checker and official rule decks on 18 intentionally introduced design-rule errors.
This matters because an AI training dataset should not merely contain successful examples.
Its validation framework must reliably distinguish valid engineering results from invalid ones.
A technically verified dataset creates a stronger foundation for models expected to generate engineering outputs rather than plausible-looking pictures.
5. Five Important AI Applications Enabled by SEMI-DEV-001
The value of this dataset extends beyond semiconductor layout generation.
It provides foundational data for several areas of semiconductor AI research and development.
Application 1: Generative AI for Analog Layout Design
Imagine an engineer specifying:
"Generate a four-finger PMOS transistor with these dimensions, including the required contacts, metal connections, and guard ring."
An AI system should translate that request into valid physical geometry.
Training on parameterized, verified layouts can help models learn the relationship between device specifications and physical implementations.
SEMI-DEV-001 provides the training pairs needed to investigate this capability.
The long-term objective is AI-assisted design systems that generate candidate layouts satisfying process constraints, reducing engineering iteration.
The dataset supports research toward this outcome; production-level autonomous layout generation still requires separate system development and validation.
Application 2: Parameter-to-Geometry Foundation Models
A transistor's width, length, and finger count influence its physical layout.
Similarly, a spiral inductor's turns, diameter, and trace width determine its geometric structure.
SEMI-DEV-001 preserves these relationships.
Researchers can use the data to train models that learn how engineering parameters map into geometric structures.
This capability is relevant to both generative design and design-space exploration.
Rather than learning only a library of fixed shapes, models can learn parameter-conditioned layout generation.
Application 3: Layout-to-Netlist and Netlist-to-Layout Models
One of the most useful capabilities in semiconductor AI would be reliable translation between physical and electrical representations.
Given a layout, a model might attempt to identify its electrical components and connections.
Given a netlist, a model might propose a compatible physical layout.
SEMI-DEV-001 supplies paired geometry and electrical descriptions along with verification results.
These examples can support supervised training and evaluation of bidirectional translation systems.
Application 4: Electrical Parameter Estimation
Physical dimensions influence electrical behavior.
For example, resistor geometry affects resistance, capacitor geometry affects capacitance, and spiral geometry affects inductance.
SEMI-DEV-001 includes estimates derived from engineering formulas.
These values can serve as initial supervised learning targets for rapid electrical estimation.
Importantly, the values are analytical estimates rather than results from full electromagnetic field solvers or SPICE simulation.
They provide useful training signals for preliminary estimation tasks, not substitutes for high-fidelity electrical characterization.
Application 5: AI Agents for Electronic Design Automation
A future semiconductor design agent may perform an iterative workflow:
Interpret a device specification.
Select a target semiconductor process.
Generate an initial physical layout.
Run design-rule checks.
Examine verification failures.
Modify the layout.
Check connectivity against the electrical specification.
Produce a verified engineering deliverable.
This is more demanding than generating code or images.
It requires tool use, error interpretation, geometric modification, and repeated verification.
SEMI-DEV-001 provides realistic inputs, valid reference outputs, and verification artifacts for building and evaluating components of such agents.
It can also support the development of task-specific reinforcement-learning environments in which layout modifications are evaluated through explicit design-rule and connectivity feedback.
Such environments would need to be constructed and tested separately; the dataset supplies valuable underlying engineering examples.
6. Why Deterministic Data Generation Matters
SEMI-DEV-001 uses parameterized generators to create original layouts.
The generators derive geometry from device specifications and published process design rules.
Contacts and vias are arranged within applicable constraints. Metal regions are adjusted to meet minimum requirements. Relevant implants and markers are positioned according to the process rules.
A central architectural principle is determinism.
Given the same generator settings and process configuration, the same device layout can be reproduced.
This provides several advantages for AI development.
First, a training example can be rebuilt when a model behaves unexpectedly.
Second, verification can be repeated independently.
Third, researchers can create controlled experiments involving specific device parameters.
Fourth, new design families can be generated systematically rather than assembled through ad hoc manual collection.
Fifth, deterministic provenance enables better dataset auditing and version control.
For engineering AI, reproducibility is particularly important.
A training example is significantly more valuable when its origin, parameters, and validity can be independently examined.
7. High-Fidelity Curated Data Versus Unverified Generated Data
Xpert Systems describes its approach as High-Fidelity Curated Data for AI Model & AI Agent Training.
That distinction is important.
Generated data is not automatically high-quality training data.
A large collection of generated semiconductor layouts may contain invalid connections, manufacturing-rule violations, unrealistic configurations, or inconsistent labels.
Simply increasing dataset size does not eliminate these problems.
High-fidelity curation requires engineering rules, documented checks, consistent representations, and clear boundaries around what has been validated.
SEMI-DEV-001 demonstrates this approach through its structured device packages and verification framework.
It also illustrates an important principle for developing engineering foundation models:
The quality of the relationship between the specification, physical artifact, and verification outcome can be as important as the number of examples.
A smaller corpus with reliable engineering supervision may be more useful for certain learning objectives than a substantially larger collection of poorly characterized layouts.
For semiconductor design, validity must be a first-class dataset attribute.
8. Open Process Design Kits Make the Dataset More Accessible
Another important aspect of SEMI-DEV-001 is its use of open process design kits.
Production semiconductor layouts are often difficult to share because of intellectual-property restrictions, foundry agreements, and confidentiality obligations.
Xpert Systems developed the layouts using published rules and process resources from SKY130 and GF180MCU.
The brochure identifies Apache-2.0 and BSD-2-Clause licensing among the open resources used.
The device layouts themselves are original outputs of Xpert Systems' generators rather than copied proprietary foundry geometry.
This approach provides a practical foundation for openly documented semiconductor AI experiments and commercial dataset licensing, subject to applicable third-party license conditions.
It also enables researchers to work with recognized semiconductor design formats and open verification tools.
The result is a more accessible foundation for semiconductor AI development without requiring customers to begin by collecting confidential production designs.
9. From Semiconductor Data to AI Models, Agents, and Benchmarks
The real opportunity is not limited to providing device layouts.
It lies in the AI development ecosystem that can be built around them.
Consider four development layers.
Layer 1: Training data
Use verified geometries, SPICE netlists, device parameters, and associated metadata to train models on semiconductor structures.
Layer 2: Specialized models
Develop models for layout generation, geometry interpretation, electrical parameter estimation, and representation conversion.
Layer 3: EDA agents
Connect these models to tools capable of generating layouts, performing checks, interpreting verification results, and proposing corrections.
Layer 4: Benchmarks and evaluations
Create controlled test sets to measure whether model-generated designs satisfy manufacturing and connectivity constraints.
Potential evaluation metrics include DRC error count, connectivity correctness, dimensional accuracy, parameter adherence, regeneration consistency, and correction success rate.
These are proposed applications of the dataset, rather than claims that a complete benchmark suite or autonomous EDA agent is already included in SEMI-DEV-001.
The distinction matters.
Providing verifiable source data is the foundation. Building reliable agentic engineering systems requires additional model development, orchestration, evaluation, and validation.
10. An Expanding Semiconductor AI Data Program
SEMI-DEV-001 is part of a broader semiconductor design data initiative at Xpert Systems.
The program encompasses multiple engineering domains.
SEMI-CELL-001 — Standard-Cell Layouts
A delivered dataset containing 685 standard-cell layouts, including logic gates, latches, and flip-flops.
SEMI-DEV-001 — Analog and RF Device Layouts
The delivered 652-device collection described in this article.
SEMI-PHOT-001 — Photonic Chip Layouts
The next dataset in the program, focused on structures such as waveguides, rings, splitters, and couplers.
SEMI-BLOCK-001 — Digital Functional Blocks
A roadmap offering covering small placed-and-routed digital blocks with associated Verilog netlists.
SEMI-PKG-001 — Semiconductor Packaging
A roadmap offering covering three-dimensional STEP models, two-dimensional engineering drawings, pin maps, and bond-wire plans.
Together, these domains represent an opportunity to develop AI training resources spanning semiconductor devices, digital logic, photonic structures, physical implementation, and packaging.
The long-term vision is an interconnected engineering-data ecosystem in which AI systems learn from multiple representations of semiconductor design.
11. What the Current Release Does — and Does Not — Validate
Technical transparency is essential when developing data for engineering AI.
The SEMI-DEV-001 documentation establishes several important scope boundaries.
Electrical resistance, capacitance, and inductance values are estimates based on simplified engineering models. They are not presented as SPICE simulation results or electromagnetic field-solver outputs.
For the GF180 process, two chip-level latch-up rules, DF.13 and DF.14, are waived for standalone devices.
The open GF180 LVS deck also has a limitation when performing pin-level comparison on MIM option B. Those devices are assessed using total capacitance matching.
Dummy devices and inductor ground shields are not included in this release.
These details should be understood when selecting the dataset for a particular research objective.
For example, researchers seeking to train models on physically verified device geometry may find the collection well suited to their needs.
Researchers requiring electromagnetic simulation labels, complete chip-level sign-off, or a comprehensive RF device library would need additional data and verification.
High-fidelity training data does not mean every possible engineering property has already been validated. It means the verified properties and their limitations are explicitly documented.
That clarity is essential for trustworthy engineering AI.
12. Who Can Benefit from SEMI-DEV-001?
Several groups can use this dataset as a foundation for further development.
Semiconductor AI startups can use it to investigate generative physical-layout systems, specialized models, and EDA automation.
EDA software companies can incorporate verified layout examples into model-training workflows, internal evaluations, and experimental design assistants.
University research laboratories can use the dataset to study semiconductor representation learning, structured generation, and verification-aware AI.
Foundation model developers can use its structured geometry and metadata to investigate multimodal engineering capabilities.
Semiconductor companies and research teams can use the collection as a controlled development resource for process-aware layout automation.
The offering can also be customized.
Xpert Systems can discuss requirements for additional device types, parameter ranges, process kits, and data volumes.
13. The Broader Vision: AI That Understands Engineering Constraints
Today, many AI systems are judged by whether their outputs appear plausible.
Engineering changes that standard.
A semiconductor layout must satisfy physical rules.
A mechanical component must satisfy dimensional and geometric requirements.
A digital circuit must implement its intended logical function.
An industrial control system must operate within defined constraints.
As AI moves into these domains, training datasets must evolve.
They need to include not only examples of successful outcomes but also the structure required to establish why an outcome is correct.
SEMI-DEV-001 reflects this direction.
Each device connects an engineering specification to a physical representation and a documented validation process.
This creates a foundation for developing systems that can eventually move beyond generating plausible answers toward producing verifiable engineering artifacts.
The opportunity is considerable.
But realizing it requires disciplined data engineering, reliable verification, domain-aware model development, and transparent evaluation.
At Xpert Systems, our goal is to supply the curated engineering data needed to support that progression.
